zero dielectric constant limit to the non-isentropic compressible Euler-Maxwell systemThanks: ∗Corresponding author

Song Jiang Address: Institute of Applied Physics and Computational Mathematics, P.O. Box 8009, Beijing 100088, P.R. China Email address: jiang@iapcm.ac.cn and Fucai Li∗ Address: Department of Mathematics, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210093, P.R. China Email address: fli@nju.edu.cn
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this paper we investigate the zero dielectric constant limit to the non-isentropic compressible Euler-Maxwell system. We justify this singular limit rigorously in the framework of smooth solutions and obtain the non-isentropic compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations as the dielectric constant tends to zero.

Key words and phrases: 
non-isentropic compressible Euler-Maxwell system, non-isentropic compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations, zero dielectric constant limit, nonlinear energy method
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
76W05, 35Q60, 35B25

1. Introduction and Main Results

The electromagnetic dynamics is governing by a coupled PDE system describing the behavior of an electrically conducting fluid and the electromagnetic fields. In the absence of viscosity, Hall effect, and heat conductivity, the system of electromagnetic dynamics can be written as ([8, 5])

∂tρ+div⁡(ρ​𝐮)=0,\displaystyle{\partial}_{t}\rho+{\rm div\,}(\rho{\bf u})=0, (1.1)
ρ⁡(∂t𝐮+𝐮⋅∇𝐮)+∇p=ρe​𝐄+μ0​𝐉×𝐇,\displaystyle\rho({\partial}_{t}{\bf u}+{\bf u}\cdot\nabla{\bf u})+\nabla p=\rho_{\textrm{e}}{\bf E}+\mu_{0}{\bf J}\times{\bf H}, (1.2)
ρ​θ​(∂tS+𝐮⋅∇S)=(𝐉−ρe​𝐮)⋅(𝐄+μ0​𝐮×𝐇),\displaystyle\rho\theta({\partial}_{t}S+{\bf u}\cdot\nabla S)=({\bf J}-\rho_{\textrm{e}}{\bf u})\cdot({\bf E}+\mu_{0}{\bf u}\times{\bf H}), (1.3)
ϵ​∂t𝐄−curl​𝐇+𝐉=0,\displaystyle\epsilon{\partial}_{t}{\bf E}-{\rm curl\,}{\bf H}+{\bf J}=0, (1.4)
∂t𝐇+1μ0​curl​𝐄=0,\displaystyle{\partial}_{t}{\bf H}+\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}{\rm curl\,}{\bf E}=0, (1.5)
∂t(ρe)+div​𝐉=0,\displaystyle{\partial}_{t}(\rho_{\textrm{e}})+{\rm div\,}{\bf J}=0, (1.6)
ϵ​div​𝐄=ρe,div​𝐇=0.\displaystyle\epsilon{\rm div\,}{\bf E}=\rho_{\textrm{e}},\quad{\rm div\,}{\bf H}=0. (1.7)

Here the unknowns ρ,𝐮=(u1,u2,u3)∈ℝ3,S,𝐄=(E1,E2,E3)∈ℝ3,𝐇=(H1,H2,H3)∈ℝ3\rho,{\bf u}=(u_{1},u_{2},u_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3},S,{\bf E}=(E_{1},E_{2},E_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3},{\bf H}=(H_{1},\linebreak H_{2},H_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, and ρe\rho_{\textrm{e}} denote the density, velocity, entropy, electric field, magnetic field, and electric charge density, respectively. The current density 𝐉{\bf J} is expressed by Ohm’s law, i.e.,

𝐉−ρe​𝐮=σ⁡(𝐄+μ0​𝐮×𝐇).\displaystyle{\bf J}-\rho_{\textrm{e}}{\bf u}=\sigma({\bf E}+\mu_{0}{\bf u}\times{\bf H}). (1.8)

The pressure pp and the entropy SS satisfy the Gibbs relation

θ​d​S=d​e+p​d​(1ρ),\theta\mathrm{d}S=\mathrm{d}e+p\,\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{1}{\rho}\right), (1.9)

where θ\theta and ee denote the temperature and the internal energy of the fluid.

To the authors’ best knownledge, the only mathematical result on the system (1.1)–(1.7) was obtained by Kawashima [14] who established the global existence of smooth solutions in whole space ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} when the initial data are a small perturbation of some given constant state. On the other hand, as it was pointed out in [8], the assumption that the electric charge density ρe≃0\rho_{\textrm{e}}\simeq 0 is physically very reasonable for the study of plasmas. In this situation, we can eliminate the terms involving ρe\rho_{\textrm{e}} in (1.1)–(1.7) and then obtain the following non-isentropic compressible Euler-Maxwell system:

∂tρ+div⁡(ρ​𝐮)=0,\displaystyle{\partial}_{t}\rho+{\rm div\,}(\rho{\bf u})=0, (1.10)
ρ⁡(∂t𝐮+𝐮⋅∇𝐮)+∇P=μ0​𝐉×𝐇,\displaystyle\rho({\partial}_{t}{\bf u}+{\bf u}\cdot\nabla{\bf u})+\nabla P=\mu_{0}{\bf J}\times{\bf H}, (1.11)
ρ​θ​(∂tS+𝐮⋅∇S)=𝐉⋅(𝐄+μ0​𝐮×𝐇),\displaystyle\rho\theta({\partial}_{t}S+{\bf u}\cdot\nabla S)={\bf J}\cdot({\bf E}+\mu_{0}{\bf u}\times{\bf H}), (1.12)
ϵ​∂t𝐄−curl​𝐇+𝐉=0,\displaystyle\epsilon{\partial}_{t}{\bf E}-{\rm curl\,}{\bf H}+{\bf J}=0, (1.13)
∂t𝐇+1μ0​curl​𝐄=0,div​𝐇=0\displaystyle{\partial}_{t}{\bf H}+\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}{\rm curl\,}{\bf E}=0,\quad{\rm div\,}{\bf H}=0 (1.14)

with

𝐉=σ⁡(𝐄+μ0​𝐮×𝐇).\displaystyle\quad{\bf J}=\sigma({\bf E}+\mu_{0}{\bf u}\times{\bf H}). (1.15)

Formally, if we take the dielectric constant ϵ=0\epsilon=0 in (1.13), i.e., the displacement current is negligible, then we obtain 𝐉=curl​𝐇{\bf J}={\rm curl\,}{\bf H}. Thanks to (1.15), we can eliminate the electric field 𝐄{\bf E} in (1.11), (1.12) and (1.14), and finally obtain that

∂tρ+div⁡(ρ​𝐮)=0,\displaystyle{\partial}_{t}\rho+{\rm div\,}(\rho{\bf u})=0, (1.16)
ρ⁡(∂t𝐮+𝐮⋅∇𝐮)+∇P=μ0​curl​𝐇×𝐇,\displaystyle\rho({\partial}_{t}{\bf u}+{\bf u}\cdot\nabla{\bf u})+\nabla P=\mu_{0}{\rm curl\,}{\bf H}\times{\bf H}, (1.17)
ρ​θ​(∂tS+𝐮⋅∇S)=1σ​|curl​𝐇|2,\displaystyle\rho\theta({\partial}_{t}S+{\bf u}\cdot\nabla S)=\frac{1}{\sigma}|{\rm curl\,}{\bf H}|^{2}, (1.18)
∂t𝐇−curl⁡(𝐮×𝐇)=−1σ​μ0​curl​(curl​𝐇),div​𝐇=0.\displaystyle\partial_{t}{\bf H}-{\rm curl\,}({\bf u}\times{\bf H})=-\frac{1}{\sigma\mu_{0}}{\rm curl\,}({\rm curl\,}{\bf H}),\quad{\rm div\,}{\bf H}=0. (1.19)

The equations (1.16)–(1.19) is called non-isentropic compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations with infinite Reynolds number which is used in describing some local processes in the cosmic system [6].

The above formal derivation is usually referred as magnetohydrodynamic approximation [8, 5]. In [15, 16], Kawashima and Shizuta justified this limit process rigorously to the complete magnetohydrodynamic fluid system in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} for local and global small smooth solutions (small perturbations of some give constant state), respectively. In [12], we studied the magnetohydrodynamic approximation for the isentropic electromagnetic fluid system in three-dimensional period domain and obtained the isentropic compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations with explicit convergence rates. Recently, we extended the results in [12] to the complete magnetohydrodynamic fluid system and obtained the full compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations [13]. We remark that the viscosities (including the shear and buck viscosities and heat conductivity coefficient) play a crucial role in the proof process of [13] and the inviscid case is left as an open problem there.

The purpose of this paper is to solve this problem and give a rigorous derivation of the compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations (1.16)–(1.19) from the non-isentropic compressible Euler-Maxwell system (1.10)–(1.15) as the dielectric constant ϵ\epsilon tends to zero. As in [13], we consider the system (1.10)–(1.15) in a periodic domain of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, i.e., the torus 𝕋3=(ℝ/(2​π​ℤ))3\mathbb{T}^{3}=(\mathbb{R}/(2\pi\mathbb{Z}))^{3}.

Below we take the harmless physical constants σ\sigma and μ0\mu_{0} to be one for simplicity of presentation. For the system (1.10)–(1.15), it is more convenient to using the pressure pp instead of the density ρ\rho as an unknown. Thus we reconsider the equations of state as functions of SS and pp, i.e., ρ=r⁡(S,p)\rho=r(S,p) and θ=Θ⁡(S,p)\theta=\Theta(S,p) for some positive smooth functions rr and Θ\Theta defined for all SS and p>0p>0, and satisfying ∂r⁡(S,p)∂p>0\frac{\partial r(S,p)}{\partial p}>0. Moreover, in order to emphasize the unknowns depending on the small parameter ϵ\epsilon, we add the superscripts ϵ\epsilon to the unknowns (p,𝐮,S,𝐄,𝐇)(p,{\bf u},S,{\bf E},{\bf H}) and rewrite the Euler-Maxwell system (1.10)–(1.15) as

a⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)​(∂tpϵ+𝐮ϵ⋅∇pϵ)+div​𝐮ϵ=0,\displaystyle a(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon})(\partial_{t}p^{\epsilon}+{\bf u}^{\epsilon}\cdot\nabla p^{\epsilon})+{\rm div\,}{\bf u}^{\epsilon}=0, (1.20)
r⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)​(∂t𝐮ϵ+𝐮ϵ⋅∇𝐮ϵ)+∇pϵ=(𝐄ϵ+𝐮ϵ×𝐇ϵ)×𝐇ϵ,\displaystyle r(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon})(\partial_{t}{\bf u}^{\epsilon}+{\bf u}^{\epsilon}\cdot\nabla{\bf u}^{\epsilon})+\nabla p^{\epsilon}=({\bf E}^{\epsilon}+{\bf u}^{\epsilon}\times{\bf H}^{\epsilon})\times{\bf H}^{\epsilon}, (1.21)
b⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)​(∂tSϵ+𝐮ϵ⋅∇Sϵ)=|𝐄ϵ+𝐮ϵ×𝐇ϵ|2,\displaystyle b(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon})(\partial_{t}S^{\epsilon}+{\bf u}^{\epsilon}\cdot\nabla S^{\epsilon})=|{\bf E}^{\epsilon}+{\bf u}^{\epsilon}\times{\bf H}^{\epsilon}|^{2}, (1.22)
ϵ​∂t𝐄ϵ−curl​𝐇ϵ+(𝐄ϵ+𝐮ϵ×𝐇ϵ)=0\displaystyle\epsilon{\partial}_{t}{\bf E}^{\epsilon}-{\rm curl\,}{\bf H}^{\epsilon}+({\bf E}^{\epsilon}+{\bf u}^{\epsilon}\times{\bf H}^{\epsilon})=0 (1.23)
∂t𝐇ϵ+curl​𝐄ϵ=0,div​𝐇ϵ=0.\displaystyle{\partial}_{t}{\bf H}^{\epsilon}+{\rm curl\,}{\bf E}^{\epsilon}=0,\quad{\rm div\,}{\bf H}^{\epsilon}=0. (1.24)

where a⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)a(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon}) and b⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)b(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon}) are defined as

a⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)=1r⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)​∂r⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)∂pϵ,b⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)=r⁡(Sϵ,pϵ)​Θ​(Sϵ,pϵ).\displaystyle a(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon})=\frac{1}{r(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon})}\frac{\partial r(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon})}{\partial p^{\epsilon}},\quad b(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon})=r(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon})\Theta(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon}). (1.25)

The system (1.20)–(1.24) are supplemented with initial data

(pϵ,𝐮ϵ,Sϵ,𝐄ϵ,𝐇ϵ)|t=0=(p0ϵ​(x),𝐮0ϵ​(x),S0ϵ​(x),𝐄0ϵ​(x),𝐇0ϵ​(x)),x∈𝕋3.\displaystyle(p^{\epsilon},{\bf u}^{\epsilon},S^{\epsilon},{\bf E}^{\epsilon},{\bf H}^{\epsilon})|_{t=0}=(p_{0}^{\epsilon}(x),{\bf u}_{0}^{\epsilon}(x),S_{0}^{\epsilon}(x),{\bf E}_{0}^{\epsilon}(x),{\bf H}_{0}^{\epsilon}(x)),\quad x\in\mathbb{T}^{3}. (1.26)

We also rewrite the target equations (1.16)–(1.19) (recall that μ0≡σ≡1\mu_{0}\equiv\sigma\equiv 1) as

a⁡(S0,p0)​(∂tp0+𝐮0⋅∇p0)+div​𝐮0=0,\displaystyle a(S^{0},p^{0})(\partial_{t}p^{0}+{\bf u}^{0}\cdot\nabla p^{0})+{\rm div\,}{\bf u}^{0}=0, (1.27)
r⁡(S0,p0)​(∂t𝐮0+𝐮0⋅∇𝐮0)+∇p0=curl​𝐇0×𝐇0,\displaystyle r(S^{0},p^{0})(\partial_{t}{\bf u}^{0}+{\bf u}^{0}\cdot\nabla{\bf u}^{0})+\nabla p^{0}={\rm curl\,}{\bf H}^{0}\times{\bf H}^{0}, (1.28)
b⁡(S0,p0)​(∂tS0+𝐮0⋅∇S0)=|curl​𝐇0|2,\displaystyle b(S^{0},p^{0})(\partial_{t}S^{0}+{\bf u}^{0}\cdot\nabla S^{0})=|{\rm curl\,}{\bf H}^{0}|^{2}, (1.29)
∂t𝐇0−curl⁡(𝐮0×𝐇0)=−curl​curl​𝐇0,div​𝐇0=0.\displaystyle{\partial}_{t}{\bf H}^{0}-{\rm curl\,}({\bf u}^{0}\times{\bf H}^{0})=-{\rm curl\,}{\rm curl\,}{\bf H}^{0},\quad{\rm div\,}{\bf H}^{0}=0. (1.30)

where a⁡(S0,p0)a(S^{0},p^{0}) and b⁡(S0,p0)b(S^{0},p^{0}) are defined through (1.25) with (Sϵ,pϵ)(S^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon}) replaced by (S0,p0)(S^{0},p^{0}). The system (1.27)–(1.30) are equipped with initial data

(p0,𝐮0,S0,𝐇0)|t=0=(p00​(x),𝐮00​(x),S00​(x),𝐇00​(x)),x∈𝕋3.\displaystyle(p^{0},{\bf u}^{0},S^{0},{\bf H}^{0})|_{t=0}=(p^{0}_{0}(x),{\bf u}^{0}_{0}(x),S_{0}^{0}(x),{\bf H}_{0}^{0}(x)),\quad x\in\mathbb{T}^{3}. (1.31)

We remark that although the electric field 𝐄0{\bf E}^{0} does not appear in the system (1.27)–(1.30), it can be induced according to the relation

𝐄0=curl​𝐇0−𝐮0×𝐇0{\bf E}^{0}={\rm curl\,}{\bf H}^{0}-{\bf u}^{0}\times{\bf H}^{0} (1.32)

by the moving conductive flow in the magnetic field.

Before stating our main results, we recall the local existence of smooth solutions to the problem (1.27)–(1.31). Since the system (1.27)–(1.30) can be written as a symmetric hyperbolic-parabolic system, the results in [26] imply that

The main result of this paper can be stated as follows.

Theorem 1.2.

Let s>7/2s>7/2 be an integer and (p0,𝐮0,S0,𝐇0)(p^{0},{\bf u}^{0},S^{0},{\bf H}^{0}) the unique classical solution to the problem (1.27)–(1.31) given in Proposition 1.1. and

for some constant L0>0L_{0}>0. Then, for any T0∈(0,T∗)T_{0}\in(0,T_{*}), there exist a constant L>0L>0, and a sufficient small constant ϵ0>0\epsilon_{0}>0 such that, for any ϵ∈(0,ϵ0]\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0}], the problem (1.20)–(1.26) has a unique smooth solution (pϵ,𝐮ϵ,Sϵ,𝐄ϵ,𝐇ϵ)(p^{\epsilon},{\bf u}^{\epsilon},S^{\epsilon},{\bf E}^{\epsilon},{\bf H}^{\epsilon}) on [0,T0][0,T_{0}] enjoying

‖(pϵ−p0,𝐮ϵ−𝐮0,Sϵ−S0,𝐇ϵ−𝐇0)​(t)‖Hs​(𝕋3)\displaystyle\|(p^{\epsilon}-p^{0},{\bf u}^{\epsilon}-{\bf u}^{0},S^{\epsilon}-S^{0},{\bf H}^{\epsilon}-{\bf H}^{0})(t)\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}
+ϵ​‖{𝐄ϵ−(curl​𝐇0−𝐮0×𝐇0)}​(t)‖Hs​(𝕋3)≤L​ϵ,t∈[0,T0].\displaystyle\qquad\quad+\sqrt{\epsilon}\left\|\left\{{\bf E}^{\epsilon}-({\rm curl\,}{\bf H}^{0}-{\bf u}^{0}\times{\bf H}^{0})\right\}(t)\right\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}\leq L{\epsilon},\ \ t\in[0,T_{0}]. (1.34)

We shall prove Theorem 1.2 by adapting the elaborate nonlinear energy method inspired by [12, 13]. The key point of the proof is to derive the error system (see (2.1)–(2.5) below) and obtain the uniform estimates in a fixed time interval independent of ϵ\epsilon. As mentioned before, the zero dielectric constant limit to the complete magnetohydrodynamic fluid system were studied in [13] where the viscosity and heat conductivity terms in the complete electromagnetic fluid system play a crucial role in the derivation of the uniform estimates. In our case, all diffusion terms disappear and we shall make full use of the special structural of the system (1.20)–(1.23) to obtain the desired uniformly estimates. A direct but crucial observation is that there is a damping term 𝐄ϵ−𝐄0{\bf E}^{\epsilon}-{\bf E}^{0} in the electric field equations which control the terms involving 𝐄ϵ−𝐄0{\bf E}^{\epsilon}-{\bf E}^{0} in the momentum equations, entropy equation, and electric filed equations. In order to obtain the desired higher order estimates to the error system, we shall also modify some ideas developed in [20, 10] which is quite different to the isentropic case [12] and the viscous non-isentropic case [13].

Remark 1.1.

The inequality (1.34) implies that the sequences (pϵ,𝐮ϵ,Sϵ,𝐇ϵ)(p^{\epsilon},{\bf u}^{\epsilon},S^{\epsilon},{\bf H}^{\epsilon}) converge strongly to (p0,𝐮0,S0,𝐇0)(p^{0},{\bf u}^{0},S^{0},{\bf H}^{0}) in L∞​(0,T,Hs​(𝕋3))L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{s}(\mathbb{T}^{3})) and 𝐄ϵ{\bf E}^{\epsilon} converges strongly to 𝐄0{\bf E}^{0} in L∞​(0,T,Hs​(𝕋3))L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{s}(\mathbb{T}^{3})) but with different convergence rates, where 𝐄0{\bf E}^{0} is defined by (1.32).

Remark 1.2.

For the local existence of solutions (p0,𝐮0,S0,𝐇0)(p^{0},{\bf u}^{0},S^{0},{\bf H}^{0}) to the problem (1.27)–(1.31), the assumption on the regularity of initial data (p00,𝐮00,θ00,𝐇00)(p^{0}_{0},{\bf u}^{0}_{0},\theta^{0}_{0},{\bf H}^{0}_{0}) belongs to Hs​(𝕋3)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}^{3}), s>7/2s>7/2, is enough. Here we have added more regularity assumption in Proposition 1.1 to obtain more regular solutions which are needed in the proof of Theorem 1.2. The higher regularity assumption on the target equations can provide a simpler arguments in this paper. To investigate the singular limit, another way is to obtain higher order uniform estimates directly, see, for example, [20] on zero Mach number limit to non-isentropic Euler equations.

Remark 1.3.

In this paper we just consider the periodic domain case, it is more interesting to study the same problem in a spatial domain with boundary which will be our future study. We remark that in this case the boundary must be analyzed very carefully, the interested reader can refer [1, 3, 2, 4, 23, 25], and among others on the zero Mach number limit of the compressible Euler equations, and [22] on singular limits of zero Alfvén number for the equations of magneto-fluid dynamics. In [3, 2], some new pioneering ideas are introduced, which can be applied to the convergence study of the singular limit in the data space, see [3, 22, 4] for the details.

Remark 1.4.

We point out that the zero dielectric constant limit is a singular limit and similar to the zero Mach number limit in some sense, see [1, 4, 9, 10, 11, 17, 20, 23, 25] and the references cited therein.

Remark 1.5.

It is obvious that if we let σ→∞\sigma\rightarrow\infty in (1.16)–(1.19), we will obtain formally the well-known ideal non-isentropic magnetohydrodynamic equations. It is interesting to establish this limit rigorously.

Before ending this introduction, we give some notations and recall some basic facts which will be frequently used throughout this paper.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we utilize the primitive system (1.20)–(1.24) and the target system (1.27)–(1.30) to derive an error system and state the local existence of solutions to the error system. In Section 3 we give a priori energy estimates to the error system and present the proof of Theorem 1.2.

3. Uniform energy estimates and proof of Theorem 1.2

In this section we shall derive the uniform decay estimates with respect to the parameter ϵ\epsilon of the solution to the problem (2.1)–(2.6) and justify rigorously the convergence of the non-isentropic Euler-Maxwell system (1.20)–(1.24) to the compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations (1.27)–(1.30). Here we shall make full use of the structure of the system (2.1)–(2.5) and Proposition 2.1, and adapt some techniques developed in [12, 13, 10, 20].

We first establish the convergence rate of the error system (2.1)–(2.4) by obtaining the a priori estimates uniformly in ϵ\epsilon. For simplicity of presentation, we define

Now we prove Theorem 1.2 by applying Proposition 3.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

By virtue of the definition of the error functions (Pϵ,𝐔ϵ,Φϵ,𝐅ϵ,𝐆ϵ)(P^{\epsilon},{\mathbf{U}}^{\epsilon},\Phi^{\epsilon},\linebreak{\mathbf{F}}^{\epsilon},{\mathbf{G}}^{\epsilon}), the regularity of (p0,𝐮0,S0,𝐇0)(p^{0},{\bf u}^{0},S^{0},{\bf H}^{0}), the error system (2.1)–(2.5) and the primitive system (1.20)–(1.24) are equivalent on [0,T][0,T] for some T>0T>0. Therefore the assumption (1.33) in Theorem 1.2 implies the assumption (3.1) in Proposition 3.1, and hence (3.2) gives (1.34). ∎
